metadata.title: RAG: Quantization & the Storage Bill
metadata.note: RAG series extension: vector quantization & storage math. Grounded in PRODUCTION_NOTES.md §1 and the 384-vs-768 result. Claude bookends + Manim body. Liam, in for Ameya (Onyx). @HumanitariansAI.

beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Ameya. Build it with Claude, then take it apart. In the project, a smaller embedding model beat a bigger one — half the storage, three times faster, and better retrieval. That's the theme today: your vectors have a price tag, and dimension is a cost decision, not just a quality one.

props.command: claude "explain vector quantization and storage math — float32 vs int8 vs binary — for a RAG index"
output: int8 is 4× smaller · binary is 32× smaller
compress to search, rescore with full vectors

beats.narration_text: Start with the one formula to know cold. Your index costs number of chunks, times dimensions, times bytes per number. In float32 that's four bytes each. A million chunks at seven-sixty-eight dimensions is about three gigabytes. Double the dimensions to fifteen thirty-six and it's six. This number is your RAM bill, and it scales with every document you add.

So dimensions cost you twice. Halve them, and you halve the storage — and you roughly halve the search time too, because every comparison is over fewer numbers. That's why a compact, well-trained model can quietly beat a larger one on the thing that matters: quality per byte. Bigger is not automatically better.
beats.visual_intent: 768 → 384: storage halved AND search ~halved; 'quality per byte'

beats.narration_text: Now shrink the numbers themselves. Scalar quantization stores each value as an eight-bit integer instead of a thirty-two-bit float — four times smaller, for a small, usually acceptable loss in recall. It's the default first move when your index gets heavy: most of the savings, very little of the pain.
beats.visual_intent: float32 → int8: 4× smaller, small recall loss; the default first move

beats.narration_text: Push it further and you get binary quantization: keep just the sign of each dimension, one bit per number. That's thirty-two times smaller — enormous savings — but the loss is real, so you never trust it alone. It's a coarse first filter, not a final answer.
beats.visual_intent: binary: 1 bit/dim, 32× smaller, bigger loss; coarse filter only

beats.narration_text: Which brings the pattern that makes aggressive compression safe: search cheap, then rescore. Use the tiny compressed vectors to pull a shortlist fast, then re-rank just those few with the full-precision vectors. You get the speed and memory of compression with almost the accuracy of full vectors. Same idea as reranking — coarse first, precise last.
beats.visual_intent: compressed search → shortlist → rescore top-k with full vectors → final; speed + accuracy

beats.narration_text: Here's where it got real in the project. A three-eighty-four dimension model scored eighty-eight percent against a larger model's seventy-six — while using half the storage and running three times faster. Better retrieval and cheaper, at once. That's the whole lesson: dimension and precision are quality and cost in the same knob.
beats.visual_intent: bar: bge/384-dim 88% vs mpnet/768-dim 76%; + half storage, 3× faster; 'better AND cheaper'

beats.narration_text: And the storage math is something you should compute before you commit, not after the bill arrives. A few lines tells you the RAM cost of a model choice up front: chunks times dimensions times bytes. Run it for float32 and int8 side by side, and the decision makes itself.

props.title: storage.py — cost a model choice up front
props.code:
def gib(n, dims, bytes_per=4):        # float32 = 4, int8 = 1
    return n * dims * bytes_per / 1e9

gib(1_000_000, 768)        # 3.07  GB  (float32)
gib(1_000_000, 384)        # 1.54  GB  (half the dims)
gib(1_000_000, 384, 1)     # 0.38  GB  (int8 → 8× off the top)

beats.narration_text: So when do you reach for this. Small index, plenty of RAM? Stay full-precision — don't add loss you don't need. Large or memory-bound? Quantize, and add a rescoring pass so you keep your accuracy. The order is always the same: measure the storage, measure the recall, then trade deliberately.
beats.visual_intent: decision: small+RAM → full precision | large/memory-bound → quantize + rescore; measure first

beats.narration_text: So keep three things. Storage is chunks times dimensions times bytes — dimension is a cost decision, not only a quality one. Int8 is four times smaller for little loss; binary is thirty-two times smaller but needs a rescore. And a smaller model can win on quality per byte — better and cheaper at the same time.

artifactLines: Storage = n × dims × bytes — dimension is a cost decision.
int8: 4× smaller, small loss · binary: 32× smaller, rescore.
A smaller model can win on quality per byte.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this prompt to your own index: compute its storage at float32 and int8, then measure recall before and after quantizing with a rescoring pass. When you can see the bytes and the recall together, you'll pick the representation that fits both your quality bar and your budget.

props.command: claude "compute my index storage at float32 vs int8, then measure recall before/after int8 + a full-vector rescore"
